title: Common Behavioral Questions
summary: The canonical bank of behavioral prompts, decoded into what each one is actually testing — so you answer the hidden question, not just the literal one.

slides.markdown:
Behavioral interviewers draw from a surprisingly small set of underlying question categories, wrapped in an almost unlimited number of specific phrasings. "Tell me about a conflict" and "describe a time two teammates disagreed and you had to step in" are the same category wearing different clothes.

The skill this topic builds isn't memorizing exact wording — it's recognizing the **category** fast enough to retrieve the right story from [your bank](crafting-star-stories), and knowing what each category is actually scoring underneath the friendly phrasing.

Each section below takes one canonical prompt, states the hidden test, and shows what separates an answer that passes it from one that just answers the words on the surface.

slides.subTitle: What almost every prompt reduces to
slides.markdown:
Nearly every behavioral question an interviewer asks maps onto one of these:

| Category | What it's really probing | Typical phrasing |
|---|---|---|
| **Conflict** | how you handle interpersonal friction without damaging trust | "tell me about a disagreement with a coworker" |
| **Failure** | accountability and whether you actually changed after | "tell me about a time you failed" |
| **Leadership** | driving outcomes without a reporting line | "tell me about a time you led without authority" |
| **Ambiguity** | judgment when the right answer isn't given to you | "tell me about a decision with incomplete information" |
| **Prioritization** | trade-off reasoning under real constraints | "tell me about competing deadlines" |
| **Influence** | changing someone's mind with evidence, not rank | "tell me about convincing a skeptical stakeholder" |

Most interviewers pick 4–6 of these per loop, one prompt each, and expect each to map to a *different* story from your bank — reusing the same story for two categories in one loop is a visible red flag.

slides.sectionTitle: "Tell me about a conflict with a coworker"
slides.markdown:
The literal question is about the conflict. The actual test is: **can you disagree with someone and end the story with a working relationship still intact?**

A weak answer either avoids conflict entirely ("I don't really have conflicts, I just try to get along") or resolves it by capitulating with no real friction shown. Neither demonstrates the skill.

A strong shape: "A teammate and I disagreed on whether to build a shared library or let two teams each build their own version. I laid out the maintenance cost of duplication with a concrete number — we already had three near-duplicate retry wrappers — and asked what would change their mind rather than repeating my point. They agreed once I offered to own the first migration myself so it wasn't extra work on their plate." That answer shows disagreement (task conflict), evidence, and a resolution that didn't require either side to lose face.

What scores it low: describing the other person as simply wrong, or a resolution where you just deferred with no substantive exchange.

slides.sectionTitle: "Tell me about a time you failed"
slides.markdown:
This question is not looking for your worst catastrophe — it's testing **accountability**: can you name your own specific error without deflecting to the team, the requirements, or bad luck.

A strong shape: "I shipped a config change to increase a connection pool size without checking the downstream database's max-connections limit. Under peak load it hit the ceiling and caused a 20-minute partial outage. I hadn't checked because I assumed the pool size was purely our side to tune — it wasn't. I rolled back within six minutes of the first alert, and afterward added a pre-deploy check that diffs any resource-limit change against the downstream service's documented ceiling." The failure is real, the cause is owned in one clear sentence, and the ending shows a concrete process change — not just "I learned to be more careful."

The giveaway of a bad answer: "we underestimated the timeline" — a team-level, causeless failure with no fingerprint of a specific decision you made.

slides.sectionTitle: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager"
slides.markdown:
This tests **judgment under a power gradient** — do you push back with evidence when it matters, or do you either cave immediately or dig in past the point it's useful.

A strong shape: "My manager wanted to ship a feature flag rollout to 100% of users in one step to hit a launch date. I proposed a staged rollout — 5%, then 25%, then 100% over three days — because the feature touched billing, and showed the incident-cost math: a bad billing bug at 100% could mean refund processing for the full user base versus 5%. She agreed to a compressed two-day version of the staged plan, which still hit the date. On day one at 5% we did catch a currency-rounding bug that would have hit every user at full rollout."

The test isn't whether you won — it's whether you disagreed **with a reason and a way to verify it**, and adapted once new information (her deadline constraint) came in, rather than treating your first proposal as non-negotiable.

slides.sectionTitle: "Tell me about a decision with incomplete information"
slides.markdown:
This tests **judgment under ambiguity** — whether you can commit to a defensible call when the data you'd want doesn't exist, instead of stalling or guessing blindly.

A strong shape: "We needed to pick a database for a new feature with a two-week deadline, and we didn't have real traffic numbers yet since the product hadn't launched. Rather than wait for data that didn't exist, I estimated worst-case load from the marketing team's user projections, picked Postgres because it could handle that ceiling with headroom and we already had operational experience with it, and explicitly documented the assumption so we could revisit it once real traffic came in. Three months later actual load was 40% of the estimate, well within what we'd chosen for."

What separates this from a lucky guess: the estimate was reasoned from an available proxy, the choice had a clear fallback plan (revisit once real data existed), and the assumption was written down rather than left implicit — which is what makes it a defensible decision rather than a coin flip that happened to land right.

slides.sectionTitle: "Tell me about a time you influenced without authority"
slides.markdown:
This tests whether you can move **people you don't manage** toward an outcome — the leadership signal that matters at every level once you're not solely executing your own tickets.

A strong shape: "Our team's deploys were breaking another team's downstream service about once a month because we didn't publish a changelog for our internal API. I had no authority over either team's roadmap. I wrote up the last three incidents with their actual cost — roughly 6 engineer-hours each in cross-team debugging — and proposed a lightweight changelog check in CI that would fail a PR if a breaking schema change shipped without a changelog entry. I got one skeptical senior engineer on the other team to co-review the proposal before pitching it to both leads, which mattered more than the technical design itself. It's been running eight months with zero repeat incidents."

The scored elements are specific: a real problem with a cost attached, a concrete ask, and — critically — getting a peer's buy-in before going to leadership, which is the actual mechanic of influence without a reporting line. [The next topic in this group](leadership-and-influence-without-authority) goes deep on that mechanic.

This one looks like an easy warm-up question, but it's testing **what you value and how you measure impact** — the answer reveals your bar for what "good" looks like more than any other prompt in the loop.

A weak answer picks the biggest-sounding project regardless of your actual role in it ("I was on the team that launched X, which grew to 10 million users") — impressive-sounding, but it says nothing about you specifically, and an interviewer will immediately follow up with "what did you do on it."

A strong answer picks the project where your personal judgment call had the clearest fingerprint on the outcome, even if the project itself was modest in scale: "My proudest work is a data-validation layer I built after noticing three separate incidents traced back to malformed upstream events. It's not a flashy feature, but it's caught over 200 bad events before they reached production in the year since, and two other teams have since copied the pattern into their own pipelines." Scale matters less here than a candidate's ability to explain, specifically, why *this* one and not a bigger-sounding alternative.

slides.subTitle: IC versus staff+
slides.markdown:
The same prompt draws a different "good" answer depending on the candidate's level:

| Prompt | Strong IC answer | Strong staff+ answer |
|---|---|---|
| "A time you disagreed with your manager" | Pushed back on a technical approach with evidence, adapted when overruled | Pushed back on a *roadmap priority* affecting multiple teams, backed by cross-team cost data |
| "A time you influenced without authority" | Got one peer team to adopt a tool you built | Got a norm or standard adopted **org-wide**, without owning any of the teams involved |
| "Your proudest achievement" | A feature or fix with a clear, bounded personal contribution | Something whose main value is that other teams copied the pattern, i.e. leverage beyond your own output |

The interviewer isn't grading a different rubric per level — they're calibrating whether the **scope** of your judgment and influence matches the scope of the role you're interviewing for. An IC-scoped answer to a staff loop reads as under-leveled even if it's a genuinely good story.

slides.sectionTitle: Answering the words instead of the test
slides.markdown:
The most common miss on canonical questions isn't a bad story — it's answering the **literal wording** while missing what's actually being scored.

Asked "tell me about a conflict," a candidate describes a disagreement that was purely technical and resolved via a shared doc with no real friction — technically a "conflict," but it demonstrates nothing about handling interpersonal tension. Asked "tell me about a failure," a candidate describes a bug that got caught in code review before shipping — nothing actually failed, so there's no accountability to show.

Both answers are responsive to the literal question and score poorly anyway, because the interviewer is pattern-matching against the hidden test (interpersonal friction handled well; a real mistake owned and corrected), not the surface words. Before answering, silently name the category and the hidden test to yourself, then pick the story that hits *that*, not just a story containing the keyword.

slides.sectionTitle: When the prompt isn't on this list
slides.markdown:
You will get a prompt that isn't a clean match to any of the six categories — "tell me about a time you had to learn something completely new fast," say. The fix isn't panic; it's decomposition.

Ask yourself: which of the six underlying skills is this actually testing, even if the wording is novel? "Learning something new fast" is usually **ambiguity** wearing a different costume — you didn't have the information (the new domain) and had to make progress anyway. "Tell me about representing your team in a decision above your level" is usually **influence** or **leadership**, depending on whether you were persuading peers or setting direction.

Once you've named the closest underlying category, retrieve the story from your bank tagged to that category rather than searching for a story that literally matches the surface wording — the categorization skill from this topic is what makes an unfamiliar prompt tractable instead of a cold start.
